course.description: Most people use AI to work faster. But the highest-leverage moves aren't about speed — they're about multiplying your team and sharpening your judgment. This guide covers two underrated AI strategies from Nathan Mapp, CPA: using AI to uplift everyone around you, and using AI to stress-test your own thinking.
learningOutcomes: Apply the methods taught in Two AI Power Moves Most People Overlook.

modules.description: Stop hoarding AI skills — the real leverage is making your whole team 10x

lessons.content:
Feel like AI has made you 10x more productive? Great. But here's the trap most people fall into:

They keep obsessively teaching **themselves** new tools instead of teaching their team.

Do the math:
- **You alone with AI** = 10x you + your team of 5 at 1x each = **15x total** (really just 11x improvement)
- **You sharing AI with your team** = everyone at 10x = **50x total**

The difference between hoarding AI skills and sharing them is the difference between a marginal personal boost and a transformational team multiplier.

Stop optimizing yourself. Start multiplying your team.
lessons.title: The 10x Trap

activities.title: How to Do It — A Practical Example

lessons.content:
Here's what this looks like in practice:

Say you built an AI tool that exports a Stripe report and uses an API from your sales system to allocate items by product line. Awesome — it saves you hours.

Now ask: **what other tasks follow this same pattern?**

Maybe Janet in payroll does a similar manual allocation of wages by product line. Schedule 30 minutes with Janet. Show her your tool. See if she can apply the same approach to her payroll allocations.

**The steps:**
1. **Identify the pattern** in what you built — not the specific task, but the type of work (e.g., "pull data from system A, allocate across categories using rules from system B")
2. **Scan your team** for who does similar work
3. **Schedule a short session** (30 min is plenty) to walk them through it
4. **Let them adapt it** to their own use case

This also has a hidden benefit: it stress-tests whether your AI productivity gains are real and durable, or if you were just chasing shiny objects.
lessons.title: How to Do It — A Practical Example

modules.title: Power Move #1: Multiply Your Team With AI

modules.description: Turn AI's confident wrongness into your secret weapon for sharper thinking

activities.title: Why AI's Confident Wrongness is Actually Useful

lessons.content:
It's easier (and feels good) to have AI push in the same direction as you. But have you noticed something? When AI gets things wrong, it does so **confidently** and in a way that's hard to refute — unless you really know what you're talking about.

Most people see this as a flaw. It's actually a feature.

You've just unlocked a **simulator for high-stakes arguments, negotiations, and critical thinking.**

AI models are built to be agreeable — they go through post-training processes that directly or indirectly train them to coddle users and give sycophantic responses. They're incentivized to keep you happy and engaged and using tokens.

That has no place in work where dollars are at stake and sound judgment is required. The fix? **Tell AI to disagree with you on purpose.**
lessons.title: Why AI's Confident Wrongness is Actually Useful

lessons.content:
This technique uses two separate AI chat windows to create genuine intellectual friction:

**Step 1:** Open **Chat Window A**. State your opinion and situation clearly.

**Step 2:** Ask Chat A to generate a killer prompt — one that tasks an AI with arguing **against** your position until it achieves victory.

**Step 3:** Open **Chat Window B** (fresh, clean context). Paste the adversarial prompt from Step 2. Now argue your position against it.

**What happens:**
- You might become genuinely convinced you were wrong (or partly wrong)
- You strengthen your ideas while gaining reps defending them against confidently-argued opposition
- You discover new perspectives or mental connections you wouldn't have reached alone

The hardest part? It's genuinely unpleasant sometimes. The AI will craft arguments so cleverly organized (but deceitfully wrong) that it feels like hard work to think of a counter. **That discomfort is the point.** That's where the thinking happens.
lessons.title: Method 1: The Two-Window Debate

lessons.content:
If you use Claude Code (or any tool with system instructions), add this to your configuration:

```
State the best-supported truth.
Name problems directly.
When you see something I don't, say so.
Be a source of honest friction, not comfort.

If an output recommends or evaluates: Reason through the strongest 
counterargument before delivering the resolved position. 
Otherwise, just deliver.
```

This turns every interaction into a more rigorous one. Instead of AI cheerfully agreeing with your first draft, it pushes back before finalizing.

**Quick-fire challenge prompts you can use anytime:**
- "What would a jaded and selective prospective customer say about this?"
- "What would a conservative and risk-averse investor say about this?"
- "What would a competitor that is 2 steps ahead of me say about this?"
- "What would a savvy and commercially-minded VP of Finance say about this?"
- "What would a rigorous and technical corporate controller say about this?"

In a world where AI makes it free to turn shallow thoughts into polished outputs, your ability to embrace discomfort and do the real thinking is what sets you apart.
